title: Full relative factorization and generic fibre of finite normalizations
statement:
Let $k$ be a field, let $S$ be a normal integral finite-type $k$-scheme with function field $K=k(S)$, and let $f:X	o S$ be dominant, where $X$ is integral of finite type over $k$. Suppose the generic fibre $X_K$ is geometrically integral. Put $F=k(X)$. Let $L/F$ be a finite separable extension and $E/K$ a finite separable subextension of $L/K$, with the given inclusions of $F$ and $E$ in $L$ agreeing on $K$. Put $T=\operatorname{Nor}_E(S)$, $Y=\operatorname{Nor}_L(X)$ and $W=X	imes_ST$. There is exactly one morphism $g:Y	o T$ satisfying $q\circ g=f\circ
u$ and inducing the specified embedding $E\hookrightarrow L$, where $q:T	o S$ and $
u:Y	o X$ are the normalization maps. The induced morphism $h=(
u,g):Y	o W$ is finite surjective. The algebra $F\otimes_KE$ is a field, its multiplication map into $L$ is injective, and the fibre of $W	o X$ at the generic point of $X$ is $\operatorname{Spec}(F\otimes_KE)$. The map $g$ is dominant. Under the canonical identification $k(T)=E$, its generic fibre $Y	imes_T\operatorname{Spec}E$ is canonically isomorphic to the normalization of $X_K$ in $L$ with the $E$-structure induced by $E\hookrightarrow L$; this isomorphism commutes with the maps to $X_K$ and induces the identity on $L$.

Normal means that every local ring is an integrally closed domain. Dominant means having dense image. Finite separable means finite-dimensional with separable minimal polynomials. The notions used are [def-weil-field], [def-pc-integral-scheme], [def-weil-finite-type-morphism], [def-sc-function-field], [def-pc-field-extension], [def-pc-geometrically-irreducible], [def-fin-normalization-extension], [def-weil-finite-integral-morphism], [def-pc-fibre-product].

source.place: Tag 0F32 (lemma-quasi-finite-Noetherian-universally-open), applied through lem-sfb-finite-dominant-normal-base-universally-open; algebra.tex Tag 0307 (lemma-integral-closure-localize). Agent affine factorization and dense generic-point argument, followed by localization identification of the generic fibre, supporting de Jong §§3.2 and 3.5 (local PDF WANTED).

proof.text: Apply the finite-normalization model theorem to $(S,K,E)$ and $(X,F,L)$. It gives integral normal $T,Y$, function fields $E,L$, finite surjective $q,\nu$, and Noetherian $S,T,X,Y$. Fix a nonempty affine $U=\operatorname{Spec}A\subseteq S$ and a nonempty affine $V=\operatorname{Spec}B\subseteq f^{-1}(U)$. Dominance makes $A\to B$ injective. The affine fraction-field theorem identifies $\operatorname{Frac}(A)=K$ and $\operatorname{Frac}(B)=F$. Write $C=\operatorname{IntCl}_A(E)$ and $D=\operatorname{IntCl}_B(L)$; the normalization definition gives $T_U=\operatorname{Spec}C$ and $Y_V=\operatorname{Spec}D$.

source.place: Affine normalization construction, with the existing finite-normalization model theorem; morphisms.tex Tag 01RV (lemma-integral-scheme-rational-functions) for the generic fields.

proof.text: The specified embedding $E\hookrightarrow L$ sends $C$ into $D$: an element of $C$ satisfies a monic polynomial over $A$, hence the same polynomial over $B$. Thus the inclusion $C\to D$ defines $Y_V\to T_U$ over $U$. These maps agree on overlaps. Indeed, on principal restrictions of an affine chart the integral closures are the corresponding localizations by Tag 0307, and the maps remain the same inclusions into $L$. On intersections of base charts first choose smaller affine base opens; their preimages are covered by affine source opens. Localization identifies every restricted normalization ring with its closure in the same field, so on these refinements both maps are the same inclusion into $L$. Consequently they glue to $g:Y\to T$, with $qg=f\nu$. Any other map with these properties must on $Y_V$ give a ring map $C\to D$ whose composite with the injection $D\hookrightarrow L$ is the specified embedding of $C\subseteq E$. It is therefore this inclusion, proving uniqueness. In particular $g$ maps the generic point of $Y$ to that of $T$, since the inverse image of $(0)\subset D$ in $C$ is $(0)$. This proves dominance and the required embedding on function fields.

source.place: Tag 0307 (lemma-integral-closure-localize); affine construction of the relative map and its uniqueness, written out here.

proof.text: The fibre-product universal property gives $h=(\nu,g):Y\to W$. Over $V\subseteq f^{-1}(U)$ its target chart is $V\times_U T_U=\operatorname{Spec}(B\otimes_A C)$ by the affine fibre-product theorem, and its inverse image is exactly $Y_V=\operatorname{Spec}D$. The ring map is $b\otimes c\mapsto bc$. A finite list generating $D$ as a $B$-module, which exists since $\nu$ is finite, also generates it as a $B\otimes_A C$-module: use coefficients $b\otimes1$. These affine target charts cover $W$ and have affine inverse images, so $h$ is affine by the affine-locality theorem; on each chart $h_*\mathcal O_Y$ is the finite module $\widetilde D$, so $h_*\mathcal O_Y$ is a finite quasi-coherent $\mathcal O_W$-algebra and the definition of finite morphism shows that $h$ is finite.

source.place: Tags 01I4 (lemma-fibre-product-affine-schemes), 01JQ (lemma-fibre-product-affines); finite module generators give finiteness directly.

proof.text: Using the charts of step 1, put $H=A\setminus\{0\}$ and $B_0=H^{-1}B$. Then $\operatorname{Spec}B_0=V\times_U\operatorname{Spec}K$ is a nonempty affine open of $X_K$, and $\operatorname{Frac}(B_0)=\operatorname{Frac}(B)=F$: both $B$ and $B_0$ lie inside $F$, and every fraction of $B$ is a fraction of $B_0$. Geometric integrality makes $X_K\times_K\operatorname{Spec}E$ integral; by the affine fibre-product theorem its open subscheme over $\operatorname{Spec}B_0$ is $\operatorname{Spec}(B_0\otimes_K E)$, so, by the affine fraction-field theorem applied to this integral scheme, $B_0\otimes_K E$ is a domain once it is nonzero. It is nonzero: a $K$-linear functional $B_0\to K$ taking $1$ to $1$ gives a retraction of $E\to B_0\otimes_K E$. Localizing at $B_0\setminus\{0\}$ gives $F\otimes_K E$ by the localization-tensor theorem; each element of this multiplicative set remains nonzero, as the same argument splits $B_0\to B_0\otimes_K E$ using a functional $E\to K$. Hence this tensor product is a nonzero domain. It has finite dimension over $F$, bounded by $[E:K]$. Multiplication by any nonzero element is an injective linear endomorphism of this finite-dimensional vector space, hence surjective; it therefore has an inverse. Thus $F\otimes_K E$ is a field. The prescribed inclusions into $L$ define the unital multiplication homomorphism $a\otimes e\mapsto ae$; its kernel is a proper ideal of a field, so it is injective.

source.place: Localization-tensor identification from Tags 00DK (lemma-tensor-localization) and 00D2 (lemma-tensor-with-bimodule); geometric integrality and elementary finite-dimensional linear algebra. Schemes Tags 01I4 and 01JQ identify the chosen generic-base affine chart.

proof.text: Let $H=A\setminus\{0\}$. Tag 0307 gives $H^{-1}C=E$: it is the integral closure of $K$ in $E$, and every element of the finite extension $E/K$ is integral over $K$. Consequently $T\times_S\operatorname{Spec}K=\operatorname{Spec}E$. Associativity of the fibre-product universal property and the affine tensor description now identify the fibre of $W\to X$ over $\eta_X=\operatorname{Spec}F$ with $\operatorname{Spec}(F\otimes_K E)$. By step 4 it has exactly one point, say $w$.

source.place: Tag 0307 (lemma-integral-closure-localize); schemes.tex Tags 01I4 and 01JQ for the affine fibre over the generic point.

proof.text: The finite dominant map $q:T\to S$ has integral source and normal locally Noetherian target by step 1. The universally-open theorem therefore applies, so its base change $p:W\to X$ is open. For every nonempty open $O\subseteq W$, $p(O)$ is a nonempty open of the integral scheme $X$ and contains $\eta_X$. Thus $O$ meets $p^{-1}(\eta_X)=\{w\}$, so $w$ is dense in $W$. The generic point of $Y$ maps under $\nu$ to $\eta_X$ (on rings $B\subseteq D\subseteq L$), so $h(Y)$ contains $w$. Since $h$ is finite, the finite-closed-map theorem makes $h(Y)$ closed. A closed subset containing the dense point $w$ is all of $W$, which proves surjectivity onto the full fibre product.

source.place: Tag 0F32 (lemma-quasi-finite-Noetherian-universally-open), through the cited normal-base specialization; morphisms.tex Tag 01WN (lemma-finite-proper) gives closedness.

proof.text: On the charts of step 1, the part of $Y\times_T\operatorname{Spec}E$ over $V$ has coordinate ring $D\otimes_C E=H^{-1}D$, since $E=H^{-1}C$ by step 5. Explicitly the isomorphism sends $d\otimes(c/a)$ to $dc/a$ and its inverse sends $d/a$ to $d\otimes(1/a)$, for $a\in H$. Applying Tag 0307 to $B\subseteq L$ identifies $H^{-1}D$ with the integral closure of $H^{-1}B$ in $H^{-1}L=L$. The charts $\operatorname{Spec}(H^{-1}B)$ cover $X_K$ by the affine fibre-product description, and their fraction fields are $F$. Thus these rings are precisely the charts defining $\operatorname{Nor}_L(X_K)$. Both constructions restrict by the same inclusions and localizations inside $L$, so the chart identifications agree on affine refinements of overlaps and glue. Each chart identification fixes $H^{-1}B$ and the embedded field $E$, and induces the identity on the fraction field $L$; the glued isomorphism is therefore over $X_K$, respects the specified $E$-structure, and induces the identity on $L$, as required.

source.place: Tag 0307 (lemma-integral-closure-localize), applied to the generic-base localization; explicit tensor-localization maps and gluing.
